hints.junior: The widget crashed once on bad websocket data — and kept showing 'Something went wrong' long after the data was fine again.
hints.mid: hasError flipped to true in componentDidCatch and just stayed true. Nothing ever told the boundary to check again.
hints.staff: A caught error and a recovered error are not the same event — this boundary only implemented the first one.

hints.junior: Try 'Push malformed update' then 'Try again' in each mode — one comes back, one just repeats the same fallback.
hints.mid: Fixed mode's Try again literally re-renders the children — that's why it can crash twice in a row if you click it before the data's fixed.
hints.staff: Watch the mount timestamp in fixed mode change on every successful Try again — that's proof it's a genuine new render, not a cached view.

hints.junior: A key change or a 'Try again' button that calls resetErrorBoundary() are both ways to force React to mount the subtree fresh.
hints.mid: resetKeys does the key-bump for you — pass values that should trigger a real remount when they change, and skip wiring the comparison by hand.
hints.staff: A reset that fires on a still-broken condition should re-crash and re-catch — that's correct, not a demo bug.

hints.junior: A boundary doesn't catch errors from a broken onClick handler or a failed fetch callback — those need their own try/catch.
hints.mid: 'We have an error boundary' can be false confidence if the actual crash lives in an event handler the boundary never sees.
hints.staff: A resetKeys entry that's a fresh object or timestamp on every render will reset (and re-crash) on every render — tie it to something that only changes when the real condition does.

sections.junior: A dashboard widget kept crashing on bad data from a websocket, so the team wrapped it in an error boundary and shipped a friendly fallback message instead of a blank screen. But once the real bug got fixed a few seconds later, the widget never came back, and users were stuck looking at that fallback for the rest of their session.
sections.mid: The boundary did exactly what it was built to do, catch the error and swap in a fallback, but nothing ever told it to try rendering the real content again, so that fallback became permanent instead of temporary.
sections.staff: The tricky part is that a fallback with no reset path looks like success in review, no crash, no blank page, but it quietly turns a one time error into a permanent one for the rest of that component's life.

sections.junior: Once a boundary catches an error it just keeps showing the fallback, since nothing built in ever flips it back automatically. Recovery means giving it a reason to try again, either by changing its key so React mounts a fresh copy, or by calling an explicit reset function from a try again button.
sections.mid: Bumping the key forces React to throw away the old tree and mount a new one, which is great when you have a natural signal like a connection ID changing. Calling a reset callback from a button works when you want the user in control of the retry instead.
sections.staff: Both approaches produce a real new render attempt, not a fake fixed state, so if the underlying problem is still there, it should crash and get caught again, and that's correct behavior. The dangerous version is a reset that fires on every render for no real reason, which just loops crash after crash.

sections.junior: Push a bad update to crash the widget, then see what happens when you try to bring it back in each mode.
sections.mid: In broken mode nothing you click actually resets the caught error, so it just sits on the fallback forever. In fixed mode, try again actually attempts a fresh render, so it can succeed or fail depending on the data at that moment.
sections.staff: Notice fixed mode can crash twice if you hit try again before pushing valid data, that's the reset genuinely working, not a bug in the demo.

sections.junior: If a boundary catches an error but never gets a reason to try again, it'll show the same fallback forever even after the real problem's gone.
sections.mid: Always wire a key change or a reset callback into a boundary that's supposed to recover, not just contain the crash.
sections.staff: Reset on a real changed signal, never on an unconditional timer, and remember a boundary only ever covers render errors in the components below it.
